In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep (Ds = !); i.e., the non-predictable lowering of H following another H, which has the effect of lowering the 'ceiling' for subsequent H tone realization. Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages. new_statements.rule_in_words: Efai, like all Lower Cross languages in Connell's field sample, is a two-tone (H, L) terraced-level tone language with contrastive downstep; the primary fieldworker finds no evidence for word-level stress (rejecting Ward's verb-root stress claim for Efik) and treats LC as non-stress languages, allowing only probable phrase-level stress and stress-like marking of compound junctures, both uninvestigated.
new_statements.exceptions: Possible phrasal stress and stress marking at compound-word junctures (fn.32); Faraclas 1984b analyses phrasal stress (extra-high tone) for Obolo only. Connell 1994 p.12 repeats that tone interacts with phrasal stress but is uninvestigated outside Obolo.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is group-level (Lower Cross, Efik as exemplar), based on citation-form wordlists and sentence lists; word-level stress denied, phrase-level stress conjectured. Connell 1994 JWAL 24(1) p.10 names Efai explicitly in the two-tone + downstep statement.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statements are made at the level of the Lower Cross group ('throughout LC', 'Efik or the other LC languages'), with Efik as the explicit exemplar; Efai (efai1241, 'Efai (Efiat - Akwa Ibom, Isangele)') is one of the 19 languages in Connell's own field sample (1988 trip) and is named explicitly in the 1994 tone section, but there is no Efai-specific prosodic statement anywhere. Any catalog entry should be flagged as a group-level statement by the primary fieldworker, not an Efai-specific description.

sources.note: Efai is in the 19-language field sample (p.5, p.14). Sec. 2.2.2 p.47: throughout LC two basic tones H/L plus phonologically significant downstep; 'two-toned, terraced level languages'. pp.54-55: rejects Ward's 1933 verb-root stress for Efik, 'difficult to find any true evidence for stress'; fn.32: not asserting no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages -- likely some phrasal stress and compound-juncture stress; fn.34 calls LC 'a non-stress language'. No word-stress rule for Efai or any LC language.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 p.10: 'in all languages of the group, there are two tones, high (H) and low (L), and contrastive downstep'; Efai named among languages retaining the older system without spread-derived falling tones. No word-stress statement.
